title: Debug Logging and Diagnostic Data
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of debug logging and diagnostic data and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to debug logging and diagnostic data.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on debug logging and diagnostic data. Debug logging and diagnostic artifacts can reveal runner behavior but should be enabled deliberately and sanitized to avoid leaking environment data. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Debug Logging and Diagnostic Data matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Use the event payload, job/step logs, exit codes, runner state, permissions, and sanitized diagnostics to separate configuration failures from infrastructure failures.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Debug logging and diagnostic artifacts can reveal runner behavior but should be enabled deliberately and sanitized to avoid leaking environment data. Debug the earliest failing step first. Use the event payload, job/step logs, exit codes, runner state, permissions, and sanitized diagnostics to separate configuration failures from infrastructure failures. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Step debug logging
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Runner diagnostic logging
items.text: Choose runner labels and access boundaries that match the workload. Self-hosted machines need patching, network segmentation, secret protection, and cleanup; keep untrusted contributions away from privileged persistent runners.

items.title: Downloading logs
items.text: Start with the first failed step and its exit code, then inspect the event, conditions, permissions, tool versions, network, and runner state. Capture sanitized diagnostics and preserve evidence of the failure.

items.title: Re-running failed jobs
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Collecting diagnostic artifacts
items.text: Use an artifact for a file produced by a run, choose exact upload/download paths, set retention intentionally, and verify the downloaded file is from the intended run/job.

items.title: Keeping sensitive information out of diagnostics
items.text: Use `${{ ... }}` for workflow expressions and the correct context for the field. Treat event-derived values as data: pass untrusted text through an environment variable and quote it instead of inserting it into shell source.

content_blocks.code:
name: Add a run summary
on: workflow_dispatch
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  report:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Write summary
        run: |
          {
            echo "## Validation summary"
            echo "- Result: passed"
            echo "- Commit: $GITHUB_SHA"
          } >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
content_blocks.expected_output: The run summary includes a short status and source commit for maintainers.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run the example manually and inspect the summary. Avoid including credentials or private payloads.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Remove sensitive values from summaries before sharing run results.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to debug logging and diagnostic data. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain debug logging and diagnostic data, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Turn run status, logs, and diagnostic data into a systematic troubleshooting process.

content.task: Apply debug logging and diagnostic data to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: Debug logging and diagnostic artifacts can reveal runner behavior but should be enabled deliberately and sanitized to avoid leaking environment data.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.

content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Debug logging and diagnostic artifacts can reveal runner behavior but should be enabled deliberately and sanitized to avoid leaking environment data. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: Debug logging and diagnostic artifacts can reveal runner behavior but should be enabled deliberately and sanitized to avoid leaking environment data.

Debug the earliest failing step first. Use the event payload, job/step logs, exit codes, runner state, permissions, and sanitized diagnostics to separate configuration failures from infrastructure failures.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
